name: Rainforest Foundation US (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result at the defaults. The forest’s pandemic risk and carbon (70%) spread by world population; the patrollers’ pay to their households (30%) by where the patrollers are: Peru 291 of 400 (the 2025 report), the rest over Guyana, Brazil and Panama by the acres patrolled there.
summary: Rainforest Foundation US backs Indigenous peoples in Peru, Brazil, Guyana and Panama to secure and defend their forest: titling their land, training and paying community patrollers who act on satellite deforestation alerts, and strengthening and funding their own organisations and their global alliance. We model all of its 2025 programme spending ($9.3 million) in five branches: the forest the year's monitoring keeps in Peru's territories, where the programme is the one a randomised trial of RFUS's own work measured; the forest its thinner monitoring and organisational support keep in Guyana, Brazil and Panama; the forest its global work with the Global Alliance of Territorial Communities keeps; the forest titles won and advanced keep; and the patrollers' pay to their households. The result is about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, nearly three fifths of it a small cut in pandemic risk from forest kept, the least grounded step, three tenths the patrollers' pay and the rest the forest's carbon, which is worth little in healthy years; Peru's territories are about half of it. The biggest uncertainties are how much of the loss the patrols prevent and whether forest loss drives pandemics; every branch but Peru's territories takes the missing-data discount, and the result is mostly uncertainty (combined range about 0.002-0.06).

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.explainer: Everything Rainforest Foundation US (RFUS) and its Peruvian affiliate spent on programmes in 2025, the latest audited year. The accounts don't split it; the 2024 Form 990 (Part III) does, into its three programmes: land rights $1,287,905, rainforest protection (community monitoring, Rainforest Alert, territorial plans) $1,751,791 and strengthening Indigenous organizations (governance, administration, direct funding, the Global Alliance of Territorial Communities) $4,841,866, of $7,881,562. All three keep Indigenous forest standing, so they are branches of this one model: the territories' forest in Peru and in Guyana, Brazil and Panama (monitoring and organisational strengthening), the global work with the Global Alliance of Territorial Communities (about 14% of the money, in the 2024 Schedule F's Africa and Asia regions), titles won and advanced (16%), and the patrollers' pay. Of the 2025 programme money, $3.77 million went on partner and community costs and $2.46 million in grants.

rows.explainer: About 1.05 million hectares in Loreto and Ucayali.

rows.explainer: The four countries' acres in hectares: about 7.9 million.

rows.label: Hectares the year's work covers (territories, titles won and titles advanced)
rows.explainer: For reading only: the territories' forest under monitoring plus the land titled and the land whose titling advanced in the year (they overlap; each branch counts its own effect on them below).

rows.label: Global work: hectares held by the Indigenous and local communities of the Global Alliance of Territorial Communities' 24 countries

source.title: Woodwell Climate Research Center (2021), Significance of community-held territories in 24 countries to global climate
source.quote: customarily hold and use at least 958 million hectares (mha) of land in the 24 reviewed countries

rows.explainer: The land the alliance (GATC) speaks for, in Latin America, Africa and Asia, the reach of RFUS's global work: grants and support to GATC and its member networks outside the four countries (2024 Form 990, Schedule F: $549,616 each in Sub-Saharan Africa and in East Asia and the Pacific, about 14% of programme spending; the 2025 accounts hold $1,370,233 restricted to GATC, note 9, p. 16) and its advocacy for direct finance to these communities (the Tropical Forest Forever Facility's Indigenous mechanism, the Forest Climate Leaders' Partnership, the COP30 land pledge). It includes the four countries' territories, a small overlap at the branch's tiny effect, and land that isn't forest.

rows.label: Land: acres newly titled to Indigenous communities with RFUS's help, 2025 (Peru)

source.title: Rainforest Foundation US, 2025 Annual Impact Report

rows.explainer: Communal titles granted in 2025 in Loreto through the SI-TIERRA titling work with AIDESEP and the regional government. RFUS's own count; the 2024 Form 990 gives 75,000 acres for 20 communities the year before, so this is a steady yearly flow.

rows.label: Land: hectares newly titled in the year
rows.explainer: About 27,400 hectares.

rows.label: Land: acres whose tenure RFUS's work strengthened in 2025 (all countries, titles included)

source.title: Rainforest Foundation US, 2025 Annual Impact Report
source.quote: Land tenure security strengthened for over 2 million acres

rows.explainer: Titles won, plus steps towards titles in 2025: boundaries demarcated and georeferenced and title-extension claims filed. The report names 990,297 acres in Peru and Paramakatoi's claim in Guyana's North Pakaraimas (about 625,000 acres); the rest it doesn't break down. RFUS's own count.

rows.label: Land: hectares whose titling advanced without a title yet
rows.explainer: About 780,000 hectares.

rows.label: Livelihoods: community patrollers trained and paid in 2025

source.title: Rainforest Foundation US, 2025 Annual Impact Report

rows.explainer: Patrollers in Brazil, Peru (291 of them), Guyana and Panama, chosen by their communities and paid for the days they patrol. RFUS's own count (307 in 129 communities in 2024, Form 990 Part III).

rows.label: Livelihoods: paid patrol days per patroller a year
rows.explainer: In the trial monitors patrolled every month in response to each month's alerts (Slough et al. 2021); a patrol of a large territory by river takes several days. Our judgment five days a month, 60 a year (two to ten days a month, 24-120).

rows.label: Livelihoods: patrollers' pay per patrol day, US$

source.title: Rainforest Foundation US, Supplied with Tech, Indigenous Forest Monitors Curb Deforestation (on the 2021 PNAS trial)
source.quote: Forest monitors received a daily stipend of $8 while out on patrols.

rows.explainer: The trial's rate in Loreto in 2018-2019, in 2019 dollars (liv_stipend_2025 brings it to 2025 prices); pay differs by country (Guyana's and Brazil's wages are higher, Panama's too). Range $6-15.

rows.label: Livelihoods: patrollers' pay per patrol day, 2025 US$
rows.explainer: The trial's rate brought to 2025 prices with US consumer prices (Convention 8), about $10.

rows.label: Livelihoods: share of the pay that is a net gain to the patroller's household
rows.explainer: Patrol days take time from fishing, farming and hunting, so only part of the pay is a gain: in remote river communities with little paid work most of the pay is new cash, but the household loses some of the food its patroller would have brought in. Our judgment half (20-80%).

rows.label: Livelihoods: net income to patrollers' households in the year, US$
rows.explainer: About {{row:liv_cash_usd}}: a small part of the $3.77 million of partner and community costs, most of which pays for equipment, travel, meetings and the partner organisations' own staff (counted in the forest branches' cost, not as income).

rows.label: Livelihoods: people in the patrollers' households
rows.explainer: Patrollers × Peru's average household size (three quarters of the patrollers are in Peru); Amazonian households are larger, which spreads the same cash more thinly and hardly changes the result.

rows.label: Health: people with fewer illnesses from the forest kept
rows.explainer: 0: no study links the year's work to measured health. Less mercury from the illegal gold mining that Guyana's district councils fought, and less fire smoke in Roraima, are real but unquantified; they sit in the territories' unmodelled share.

rows.label: Wellbeing: people whose life satisfaction rises from nature kept
rows.explainer: 0: no visitors or green-space effect; the communities' own gains are the patrollers' pay and the titles' security (unmodelled share).

rows.label: Wild animals: animal-years affected
rows.explainer: 0: RFUS claims no welfare effect on wild animals, and more forest animals alive is not by itself a gain (sign unknown).

rows.label: Territories: years of protection the year's spending buys
rows.explainer: 1: an ongoing programme's yearly flow, one year of the territories' monitoring against one year's cost (Convention 3). The titles count their own years (land_years_protected).

rows.label: Climate: years until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: Patrols and support run through the year and the clearing they prevent would have happened through the same year: half a year on average (0-1).

rows.label: Years of protection, discounted
rows.explainer: Every year of protection, and the wait before it, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Forest: CO₂ released per hectare of tropical forest lost
rows.explainer: The tropics' average, 2.4 billion tonnes over 3.7 million hectares lost in 2023 (about 650 tonnes a hectare; World Resources Institute, the shared figures every forest model reads). Guyana's and the Yanomami territory's dense, old forest would raise it; Panama's more disturbed forest lower it. An average standing in as a best guess; its spread is the shared fact's range.

rows.label: Forest: share of the year's avoided loss that stays standing for good
rows.explainer: A year's support delays clearing; some of the forest kept would be cleared in a later year anyway if the threat outlasts the support. Anchors: the trial's effect shrank in its second year (−8.4 then −3.3 hectares a community, Slough et al. 2021), which argues that deterrence fades when attention moves; titled and patrolled territories do keep their forest for decades. Our judgment half (20-90%). One question only: whether the year's support prevents clearing at all is the counterfactual row.

rows.label: Territories: share of the forest lost a year without the support, Guyana
rows.explainer: Guyana loses very little forest: its national monitoring (the Guyana Forestry Commission's MRVS, Year 2020 report: https://redd.unfccc.int/uploads/2_296_guyana_mrvs_and_accuracy_assessment_report_-_year_2020.pdf) gives about 0.06% a year (0.057% in 2020) and 0.02-0.08% over two decades, most of it gold mining, the threat the district councils RFUS funds fight. Indigenous titled land in the south and the Pakaraimas sits close to the national rate. Our judgment 0.06% (0.02-0.15%).

rows.label: Territories: share of the forest lost a year without the support, Brazil
rows.explainer: The territories are in Roraima (Yanomami and Ye'kwana lands, Raposa Serra do Sol) and the Xingu: Indigenous lands in Brazil lose far less than the Amazon's 0.5-1% a year outside them, but the Yanomami territory's gold rush cleared thousands of hectares in 2019-2022 and fires burn the savanna edges. Our judgment 0.08% (0.02-0.3%), between the 0.14% Cool Earth's briefing gives for Amazonian Indigenous land on average and Guyana's.

rows.label: Territories: share of the forest lost a year without the support, Peru
rows.explainer: The trial's control communities in Loreto lost about 16 hectares each in a year (8.4 hectares was a 52% fall) on an average 6,493 hectares: 0.25% a year, our best guess; those communities were picked as threatened (their median lost 2.54% of its land in 2010-2016, about 0.4% a year, the high end). The low end is Cool Earth's 0.14% Amazon average for Indigenous land, less the safer upriver territories.

rows.label: Territories: share of the forest lost a year without the support, Panama
rows.explainer: Panama's comarcas and collective lands (Emberá, Wounaan, Guna, Darién) face cattle ranching and logging; Darién loses forest fast. Our judgment 0.3% (0.1-0.6%), like the Peruvian trial's threatened communities.

rows.label: Territories: share of the forest lost a year without the support, area-weighted
rows.formula: (ter_guy_acres * ter_guy_loss_rate + ter_bra_acres * ter_bra_loss_rate + ter_per_acres * ter_per_loss_rate + ter_pan_acres * ter_pan_loss_rate) / (ter_guy_acres + ter_bra_acres + ter_per_acres + ter_pan_acres)
rows.explainer: For reading only: about {{row:ter_baseline_loss_rate}} a year. Guyana's low rate on 60% of the area pulls it well below the Peruvian trial's 0.25%.

rows.label: Other territories: share of the forest lost a year without the support, area-weighted
rows.formula: (ter_guy_acres * ter_guy_loss_rate + ter_bra_acres * ter_bra_loss_rate + ter_pan_acres * ter_pan_loss_rate) / (ter_guy_acres + ter_bra_acres + ter_pan_acres)
rows.explainer: Guyana, Brazil and Panama by area: about {{row:tero_baseline_loss_rate}} a year.

rows.label: Territories: CO₂ that stays out of the air per hectare-year if all the loss were averted
rows.explainer: For reading only: the loss the support works against × the share kept for good × CO₂ per hectare lost, across all four countries; each territories branch computes its own below, and the share the support actually prevents is its counterfactual row.

rows.label: Peru territories: at-risk hectares a year that would be lost for good
rows.explainer: Before the share the support prevents and the other adjustments.

rows.label: Other territories: at-risk hectares a year that would be lost for good
rows.explainer: Before the share the support prevents and the other adjustments.

rows.label: Peru territories: CO₂ at stake, before adjustments
rows.explainer: Hectares lost for good a year × CO₂ per hectare × the discounted year.

rows.label: Other territories: CO₂ at stake, before adjustments
rows.explainer: Hectares lost for good a year × CO₂ per hectare × the discounted year.

rows.label: Global work: share of the alliance's land whose forest is lost a year
rows.explainer: Indigenous and community forest loses about 0.14% a year in the Amazon (Cool Earth's briefing), less in Guyana, more in parts of the Congo Basin and Indonesia; part of the 958 million hectares isn't forest. Our judgment 0.1% of the land a year (0.03-0.3%).

rows.label: Global work: at-risk hectares a year that would be lost for good
rows.explainer: Before the share the year's global work prevents and the other adjustments.

rows.label: Global work: CO₂ at stake, before adjustments
rows.explainer: Hectares lost for good a year × CO₂ per hectare × the discounted year.

rows.label: Land: a step towards a title, as a share of a title's protection
rows.explainer: Demarcation, georeferencing and filed claims bring a title closer and deter some invasion (claims are recorded), but titling in Loreto took years even after them (now 8-18 months, the report says) and Guyana's extension requests may not be granted. Our judgment a tenth of a title's effect a year (3-30%).

rows.label: Land: hectares titled, counting advanced land at its title-equivalent share
rows.explainer: About 100,000 title-equivalent hectares.

rows.label: Land: share of untitled community forest lost a year
rows.explainer: Blackman et al. (2017) find forest cover change (clearing and disturbance) of 0.37 percentage points a year in Peruvian Amazon communities before titling, clearing a part of it; the trial's Loreto control communities, 60 of 76 already titled, lost 0.25% a year. Our judgment 0.25% (0.1-0.5%) for the untitled communities in titling's pipeline.

rows.label: Land: years a title is brought forward
rows.explainer: A title is a won legal status: most of these communities would get title eventually, through the government's own programmes and other groups' help, so RFUS's work counts for the years it brings the title forward, the site's shared years for a won reform (docs/normalization.md 2.9). Titling is a steady yearly output of paid legal and mapping work (75,000 acres titled in 2024, 67,762 in 2025), so it is a unit cost like the rest of the model, not a one-off campaign win.

rows.label: Land: discounted years of protection
rows.explainer: The years brought forward, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Land: at-risk hectares a year that would be lost for good
rows.explainer: Before the share a title prevents and the other adjustments.

rows.label: Land: CO₂ at stake, before adjustments
rows.explainer: Hectares lost for good a year × CO₂ per hectare × the discounted years.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: deaths if the catastrophe happens
rows.explainer: The shared figure: WHO's 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020-2021, the pandemic the yearly chance below is defined by.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic
rows.explainer: The shared figure (Marani et al. 2021): about 2% a year.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of new diseases whose emergence land-use change drove
rows.explainer: The shared figure (IPBES 2020): more than 30% of new diseases since 1960.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of the land-use risk that scales with tropical forest loss
rows.explainer: The shared judgment (facts/catastrophe.json): half of the land-use risk scales with tropical forest loss (10-100%), anchored on Allen et al. (2017). No study has measured this dose.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: fall in the yearly pandemic chance per hectare of tropical forest kept
rows.explainer: The land-use share of new diseases × the share of it that scales with tropical forest loss × the yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic, per hectare of the tropics' yearly loss: the risk falls in proportion to the forest kept, as in the site's other forest model. The least grounded number here.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: fall in the catastrophe's yearly probability from the year's work
rows.explainer: The forest kept for good after each branch's adjustments × the risk per hectare: the fall in the yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic. For reading and the bounds check; the branches' pandemic rows carry it.
rows.formula: (terpe_lasting_loss_ha_per_year * terpe_credit + tero_lasting_loss_ha_per_year * tero_credit + glob_lasting_loss_ha_per_year * glob_credit + land_lasting_loss_ha_per_year * land_credit) * risk_per_ha_year

rows.label: Share of the catastrophe's deaths that are of children under five
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: mostly older people died, few young children.

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: school-age children were the least affected.

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: about 15% of adult excess deaths were under 50; the rest are valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: A catastrophe's deaths are valued like every death on the site, by age band × your value of a life; no premium for their number.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of every later year's healthy life the catastrophe would take
rows.explainer: The shared judgment: 0, the world recovers from a COVID-scale pandemic; its deaths are counted above.

rows.label: Discounted future years of healthy life per person of the long-run population, if the future ends now
rows.explainer: The site's one count of future generations (docs/normalization.md 2.19): the healthy years of people not yet born, discounted for ever at the shared rate. People alive now die in the catastrophe and are counted as deaths, so this stream rises from nothing to the long-run population over one lifetime (@catastrophe.life_expectancy_now) and then runs on: about 8 years at the default 4%, about 960 at the 0.1% floor. Fixed; don't edit.

rows.label: Peru territories: pandemic deaths averted, in units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The forest kept for good × the risk cut per hectare × the discounted year × the pandemic's deaths × the value of a death.

rows.label: Other territories: pandemic deaths averted, in units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The forest kept for good × the risk cut per hectare × the discounted year × the pandemic's deaths × the value of a death.

rows.label: Global work: pandemic deaths averted, in units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The forest kept for good × the risk cut per hectare × the discounted year × the pandemic's deaths × the value of a death.

rows.label: Land: pandemic deaths averted, in units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: As for the territories, over the title's discounted years.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: future years of healthy life kept, discounted
rows.formula: ((terpe_lasting_loss_ha_per_year * terpe_credit + tero_lasting_loss_ha_per_year * tero_credit + glob_lasting_loss_ha_per_year * glob_credit) * protection_years + land_lasting_loss_ha_per_year * land_protection_years * land_credit) * risk_per_ha_year * future_share_lost * @catastrophe.world_population_long_run * future_years_per_person
rows.explainer: Every later year's healthy life the pandemic would take from people not yet born, discounted for ever at the shared rate; 0 at the best guess (future_share_lost). Already credited by each forest branch.

rows.label: Health: DALYs averted per person per year
rows.explainer: 0: no health branch (health_people).

rows.label: Livelihoods: Peru's household-survey mean consumption per person, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: The household-survey mean (World Bank PIP) in 2024 US$ at market prices, as the site's other builds compute it: about $2,700 a year. Three quarters of the patrollers are in Peru; Guyana's, Brazil's and Panama's rural Indigenous households are folded into it.

rows.label: Livelihoods: patrollers' households' consumption as a share of Peru's survey mean
rows.explainer: Indigenous Amazonian communities are among the poorest in their countries, living largely from their own crops, fish and forest with little cash income. The poorest fifth in a country's survey consume about 40% of its mean, and remote Amazonian households less. Our judgment 35% (20-60%).

rows.label: Livelihoods: consumption per person a year in the partner communities, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: In US$ at market prices, the same basis as the cash, so no PPP factor is needed (2025 cash against 2024 prices; the year's US inflation, under 3%, is inside the share's range).

rows.label: Livelihoods: ln(consumption) gain per person per year
rows.explainer: The log of consumption with the net pay over without it, for each person in the patrollers' households, for the year.

rows.label: Livelihoods: the cash's value, in units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: People × the log gain × the shared value of a doubling of consumption.

rows.label: Wellbeing: life satisfaction gained per person per year (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Not reached: nature_people is 0.

rows.label: Wild animals: days of disabling pain spared per animal-year (negative if more)
rows.explainer: Not reached: wild_animal_years is 0.

rows.label: Wild animals: days of pain spared (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: no wild-animal welfare effect is counted (wild_animal_years is 0).

rows.label: Wild animals: chicken-equivalent pain days
rows.explainer: 0: the species step for wild animals, not reached here (wild_animal_years is 0).

rows.label: Peru territories: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: The effect comes from a randomised trial of this programme in this region (Slough et al. 2021), but an imprecise one: the first-year 95% interval runs from −19.4 to +2.6 hectares a community, and the six-country Metaketa trials of community monitoring found smaller effects on average, so a large point estimate likely overstates (×0.85). The loss rate and CO₂ per hectare are averages standing in as best guesses, their spread in their own ranges. 0.85 (0.5-1).

rows.label: Other territories: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: The trial's imprecise estimate (×0.85, as for Peru), carried from Loreto's river communities to Guyana's, Brazil's and Panama's territories, with other threats (gold mining, ranching) and other organisations doing the work (×0.9). 0.75 (0.45-1).

rows.label: Peru territories: share of the at-risk loss the support prevents
rows.explainer: Anchor: in the trial (Slough et al. 2021), alerts, training and paid patrols cut tree-cover loss by 52% in the first year (8.4 of about 16.2 hectares a community) and by about 21% in the second (3.3 of about 15.5 hectares: 37% over the two years), effects the authors call substantially attenuated after the first year. Most of Peru's communities in 2025 are past their first year (RFUS counts 129 communities in 2024 and more than 160 in 2025, so about a fifth are new): 0.2 × 52% + 0.8 × 21% is about 27%. Peru's 291 monitors cover about 3,600 hectares each, 1.7 times the trial's 2,200, so a little less. Indigenous territories already keep their forest far better than other land, which is in the baseline rate, not RFUS's credit. Our judgment 23% (8-45%).

rows.label: Other territories: share of the at-risk loss the support prevents
rows.explainer: About 110 patrollers cover 6.8 million hectares, some 62,000 each, nearly 30 times the trial's density, so the trial's effect can't carry over; what does more of the work here is the organisations RFUS strengthens and funds: Guyana's district councils pursuing illegal miners (arrests and equipment seized in 2025), drone mapping of a concession on community land, Roraima's fire brigades. Our judgment 8% (2-25%), a third of Peru's 23%.

rows.label: Peru territories: RFUS's share of the resources behind the forest kept
rows.explainer: Convention 2, a rough count of a year's resources behind the effect the trial measures. RFUS's: it designed and runs the programme (Slough et al. 2021: 'the NGO that designed and implemented the monitoring program'), pays the monitors (291 × about 60 days × about $10, some $175,000) and its Peru team's training, phones, alerts' delivery and travel, together roughly $0.6-0.9 million of its programme money. Others': the community assemblies' and citizen patrols' unpaid days deciding and acting on what monitors find (over 100 Peruvian communities, a few dozen person-days a month each at the same $10 a day: roughly $0.2-0.4 million), the federations' coordination (ORPIO and its members, partly RFUS-funded), and Peru's own alert platform (Geobosques), small per community. RFUS about 0.75 of 1.05 million: our judgment 70% (45-90%).

rows.label: Other territories: RFUS's share of the resources behind the forest kept
rows.explainer: Convention 2, built roughly from the resources the 2025 report names (https://rainforestfoundation.org/about/financials-transparency/2025-annual-report/, Guyana), like for like over the decade: RFUS facilitated about $7 million of combined direct and intermediated funding to the Amerindian Peoples Association and the South Rupununi District Council, from Norway's NICFI through Norad, the Swedish Postcode Foundation, Nia Tero and the Samueli Foundation; over the same decade APA's budget grew from $153,000 to $1.7 million a year (roughly $9 million in all if it grew evenly) and SRDC's to $1.1 million (roughly $6 million, our guess), about $15 million. Part of the $7 million went to the partners directly rather than through RFUS's books, which makes it the funders' resource, not RFUS's: RFUS's share of Guyana's partners is about 30-50%, say 40%. Guyana is 70% of this branch's area; Brazil's and Panama's partners (CIR, GeoIndígena and others) have their own funders and state agencies (about 30% for RFUS there), and the communities' unpaid patrols and governments' enforcement count too: 0.7 × 40% + 0.3 × 30% is about 37%. Our judgment 38% (25-75%).

rows.label: Peru territories: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: The acres are RFUS's own count of land its partners patrol, not independently checked; in the trial three of 39 communities never started (one uninterested, two unsafe to reach), and that slippage is inside the trial's effect, so the delivery gap here is the patchier cover of large territories. 90% (70-100%).

rows.label: Other territories: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: The acres are RFUS's own count of land its partners patrol, not independently checked; in the trial three of 39 communities never started (one uninterested, two unsafe to reach), and that slippage is inside the trial's effect, so the delivery gap here is the patchier cover of large territories. 90% (70-100%).

rows.label: Peru territories: benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: Negative: leakage, clearing pushed onto forest outside the communities (the trial found no displacement in buffer areas, imprecisely; studies of protected areas find from none to about 40%). Positive: the environmental-crime complaints RFUS trains communities to file, and Peru's draft national strategy for Indigenous adaptation to fires and droughts, biodiversity and water. Net 0 (−30% to +30%).

rows.label: Other territories: benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: Negative: leakage, as for Peru. Positive: less mercury from illegal mining in Guyana (SRDC now measures it in soil and fish), biodiversity and water. Net 0 (−30% to +30%); RFUS's global work is its own branch.

rows.label: Peru territories: discount for outcomes not measured
rows.explainer: 1, measured (Convention 12): RFUS's count of who got the programme (291 monitors over 2.6 million acres) meets its own randomised evaluation of the same programme, delivered the same way in the same region (Slough et al. 2021).

rows.label: Other territories: discount for outcomes not measured
rows.explainer: No evaluation of RFUS's support in Guyana, Brazil or Panama; the branch rests on the Peruvian trial, far thinner patrols and judgment (Convention 12).

rows.label: Peru territories: product of the adjustments
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Peru territories: credit, with the unmodelled share
rows.explainer: The adjustments × (1 + the unmodelled share; the side-effect slider weights that share).

rows.label: Other territories: product of the adjustments
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Other territories: credit, with the unmodelled share
rows.explainer: The adjustments × (1 + the unmodelled share; the side-effect slider weights that share).

rows.label: Global work: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: No study measures what an alliance's advocacy and finance mechanisms do to forest loss; the chain runs from secure tenure and direct finance, whose forest effects are the land and territories branches' evidence, to the whole area. 0.6 (0.3-1).

rows.label: Global work: share of the alliance land's at-risk loss the year's work prevents
rows.explainer: What a year of the alliance's work buys: finance and recognition won for its members (at least 20% of the Tropical Forest Forever Facility's payments earmarked for Indigenous peoples and local communities, with GATC co-designing the mechanism; the COP30 pledge to secure nearly 400 million acres by 2030; the 2021 Forest Tenure Funders' $1.7 billion), spread over 958 million hectares and many years, much of it still pledged, not paid. Against the territories' 8% from patrols and organisations on the ground, a tenth of a percent of the whole area's loss. Our judgment 0.1% (0.01-0.5%).

rows.label: Global work: RFUS's share of the resources behind the alliance's results
rows.explainer: Convention 2: the alliance's member networks (COIAB, AMPB, AMAN, REPALEAC and others) and their own staff, its other funders and partners (the Ford Foundation, the Rights and Resources Initiative, the Tenure Facility, Nia Tero), and the governments that negotiate the pledges, against RFUS's roughly $1-1.5 million a year (Schedule F's two regions; GATC's restricted $1.37 million). A rough count of a year's resources: RFUS about $1.3 million; the member networks' own staff and budgets for the alliance's work and its secretariat, a few million dollars (our guess: no accounts are published); the other funders' and partners' tenure and finance advocacy (the Rights and Resources Initiative and the Tenure Facility each spend several million a year), together roughly $8-15 million. RFUS about 1.3 of 12: our judgment 10% (3-30%).

rows.label: Global work: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: The Tropical Forest Forever Facility raised a few billion dollars of its $25 billion target at launch, and pledges like COP30's are not binding. 80% (50-100%).

rows.label: Global work: benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: Positive: rights recognised and finance reaching communities for their own uses, and RFUS's working group on the ART TREES carbon standard (endorsed by 30 organisations). Negative: leakage, and carbon-market rules that could let finance flow without forest kept. Net 0 (−20% to +30%).

rows.label: Global work: discount for outcomes not measured
rows.explainer: Nothing measures the global work's effect on forest (Convention 12).

rows.label: Global work: product of the adjustments
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Global work: credit, with the unmodelled share
rows.explainer: The adjustments × (1 + the unmodelled share; the side-effect slider weights that share).

rows.label: Land: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: Quasi-experimental studies, not trials: Blackman et al. (2017, Peru, panel of titled and untitled communities) and Baragwanath and Bayi (2020, Brazil, full property rights cut deforestation) find titles protect forest; BenYishay et al. (2017) find no effect of Brazil's demarcations. 0.7 (0.4-1) for the design and the mixed results.

rows.label: Land: share of the at-risk loss a title prevents while it counts
rows.explainer: Blackman et al. (2017): titling cut clearing by more than three quarters and disturbance by about two thirds in the year of title and the next, in Peru's Amazon; whether it lasts beyond two years they don't test. Brazil: full property rights cut deforestation inside Indigenous territories (Baragwanath and Bayi 2020), demarcation alone didn't (BenYishay et al. 2017). Our judgment 35% (5-70%) a year over the years counted, under the short-run Peruvian effect.

rows.label: Land: RFUS's share of the resources behind the titles
rows.explainer: Titles come from the regional government (GOREL's titling office), with AIDESEP and its regional federations filing the claims, and co-funders (Rainforest Trust in the Chambira-Marañón project); RFUS pays for the legal, mapping and georeferencing work that the 2025 report credits with cutting titling time to 8-18 months. Our judgment 40% (20-70%).

rows.label: Land: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Titles are registered legal documents, but overlapping forestry or oil concessions and weak enforcement mean some titled land stays exposed; RFUS's own counts. 90% (70-100%).

rows.label: Land: benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: Positive: secure land for the communities themselves (fewer land conflicts and invasions, access to state programmes such as Peru's conditional forest payments that require title, and the rights at stake: the Saweto leaders were murdered defending untitled land). Negative: a title can also let a community sign logging contracts (Blackman et al. note the worry). Net +10% (−20% to +50%).

rows.label: Land: discount for outcomes not measured
rows.explainer: Nobody measures the titled communities' forest against untitled ones for RFUS's titles (Convention 12).

rows.label: Land: product of the adjustments
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Land: credit, with the unmodelled share
rows.explainer: The adjustments × (1 + the unmodelled share; the side-effect slider weights that share).

rows.label: Livelihoods: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Income to poor households is valued by the site's cash-transfer evidence; the pay rate is the trial's and the days a judgment. 0.9 (0.6-1), as Cool Earth's cash.

rows.label: Livelihoods: share of the cash that wouldn't have come anyway
rows.explainer: 1: without the programme nobody pays these patrols (the trial's control communities had only unpaid citizen patrols).

rows.label: Livelihoods: RFUS's share of the resources behind the pay
rows.explainer: 1: RFUS pays the patrollers.

rows.label: Livelihoods: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Pay goes through partner organisations and community leaders; some is lost or delayed. 90% (70-100%), as Cool Earth's cash.

rows.label: Livelihoods: benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: Positive: skills (smartphones, mapping, drones) and standing in the community (the trial found monitors became recognised forest authorities). Negative: patrollers confront loggers, miners and traffickers and some are threatened; the trial found citizens joined collective patrols less once monitors were paid. Net 0 (−30% to +20%).

rows.label: Livelihoods: deaths averted by the extra income, as a share of its consumption value (at the default value of a life)
rows.explainer: The cash-income recipe's mortality ratio: GiveWell's GiveDirectly analysis puts the deaths cash averts at about a quarter of its consumption value at Kenya's under-five mortality of about 5%; Amazonian Indigenous under-five mortality is lower, about 3%, and the pay goes to adult patrollers rather than mothers.

rows.label: Livelihoods: deaths averted by the cash, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: The ratio × your value of a life, so these deaths move with it like every death on the site.

rows.label: Livelihoods: gains to others from the cash spent locally, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: A side effect: pay spent in the communities' few shops and markets raises traders' and producers' incomes. The shared figure for cash spent locally, +10% (0 to +40%).

rows.label: Livelihoods: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Nobody counts the patrol days paid or the households' consumption (Convention 12).

rows.label: Livelihoods: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The livelihoods branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Livelihoods: adjustments and unmodelled effects
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments × (1 + its unmodelled effects, the child deaths averted and the spillovers to others).

rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the five branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by its healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: Counterfactual: weighted average of the branches
rows.formula: (terpe_dalys_raw * terpe_counterfactual_adj + tero_dalys_raw * tero_counterfactual_adj + glob_dalys_raw * glob_counterfactual_adj + land_dalys_raw * land_counterfactual_adj + liv_dalys_raw * liv_counterfactual_adj) / (terpe_dalys_raw + tero_dalys_raw + glob_dalys_raw + land_dalys_raw + liv_dalys_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the five branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by its healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: RFUS's share of the resources: weighted average of the branches
rows.formula: (terpe_dalys_raw * terpe_attribution_share + tero_dalys_raw * tero_attribution_share + glob_dalys_raw * glob_attribution_share + land_dalys_raw * land_attribution_share + liv_dalys_raw * liv_attribution_share) / (terpe_dalys_raw + tero_dalys_raw + glob_dalys_raw + land_dalys_raw + liv_dalys_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the five branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by its healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by the branch's healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: Delivery: weighted average of the branches
rows.formula: (terpe_dalys_raw * terpe_implementation_adj + tero_dalys_raw * tero_implementation_adj + glob_dalys_raw * glob_implementation_adj + land_dalys_raw * land_implementation_adj + liv_dalys_raw * liv_implementation_adj) / (terpe_dalys_raw + tero_dalys_raw + glob_dalys_raw + land_dalys_raw + liv_dalys_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the five branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 1: the other resources behind the forest are in each branch's attribution share. RFUS also helps partners raise money of their own ('over $10.5 million unlocked for Indigenous-led forest protection' in 2025, the report says), which could add to the result if that money wouldn't otherwise fund forest protection; much of it comes from climate and conservation funders who would give elsewhere in the field. Range 0.85-1.1. Applied to all branches.

rows.label: Missing-data discount: weighted average of the branches
rows.formula: (terpe_dalys_raw * terpe_missing_data_adj + tero_dalys_raw * tero_missing_data_adj + glob_dalys_raw * glob_missing_data_adj + land_dalys_raw * land_missing_data_adj + liv_dalys_raw * liv_missing_data_adj) / (terpe_dalys_raw + tero_dalys_raw + glob_dalys_raw + land_dalys_raw + liv_dalys_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the five branches, for reading only.

rows.label: All adjustments combined: weighted average of the branches
rows.formula: (terpe_dalys_raw * terpe_total_adj + tero_dalys_raw * tero_total_adj + glob_dalys_raw * glob_total_adj + land_dalys_raw * land_total_adj + liv_dalys_raw * liv_total_adj) / (terpe_dalys_raw + tero_dalys_raw + glob_dalys_raw + land_dalys_raw + liv_dalys_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the five branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Effects not modelled: weighted average of the branches
rows.formula: (terpe_dalys_raw * terpe_unmodelled_benefits_adj + tero_dalys_raw * tero_unmodelled_benefits_adj + glob_dalys_raw * glob_unmodelled_benefits_adj + land_dalys_raw * land_unmodelled_benefits_adj + liv_dalys_raw * liv_unmodelled_benefits_adj) / (terpe_dalys_raw + tero_dalys_raw + glob_dalys_raw + land_dalys_raw + liv_dalys_raw)
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the five branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fossil fuel near people
rows.explainer: 0: land carbon carries no fossil-fuel smoke (conservation family); the partnerships' forest is kept from clearing and logging, not burned for fuel near cities.

rows.formula: tco2e_bridged * (($deaths_per_tco2e * $climate_heat_share * ((1 - methane_share) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -$climate_heat_death_delay + methane_share * @climate.methane_heat_deaths_vs_co2 * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ -@climate.methane_heat_death_delay) * (1 + $side_effect_weight * @climate.nondeath_damages_vs_deaths) * (@death_ages.heat_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.heat_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.heat_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.heat_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74) + ($deaths_per_tco2e * (1 - $climate_heat_share) * air_pollution_weight + extra_deaths_per_tco2e + methane_share * @climate.ozone_deaths_per_tco2e_methane / (1 + ln(1 + $discount_rate) * @climate.methane_lifetime_years)) * (@death_ages.air_pollution_share_under5 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_under5 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_5_14 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_5_14 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_15_49 * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_15_49 + @death_ages.air_pollution_share_50plus * @moral_weights.uov_per_death_age_50_74)) * $life_value_multiplier) / ($uov_per_daly)
